{"id": "16d5b250-d056-490f-98ec-f1fa6ea2f157", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "There's no dedicated skill for a full EKS compliance scan, so I'm treating this as a bounded but large task best handled by delegating to sub-agents rather than digging for root cause myself. I'm aware sub-agents are read-only and may only have use_aws rather than kubectl access, so I'll plan for the Kubernetes-focused sub-agent to use kubectl if available and otherwise flag any checks it can't verify. I'm also pulling together the CIS EKS Benchmark v1.8.0 control list to map out exactly which items each sub-agent should check against, covering audit logging, kubeconfig permissions, and kubelet configuration settings.

I'm continuing through the benchmark sections — API server authentication/authorization settings, RBAC and pod security standards, network policies, secrets management, namespace isolation, and ECR/image scanning controls — so I can divide these checks sensibly across the sub-agents I'm about to spawn.

I'm thinking of splitting the work into separate sub-agents: one covering the AWS control-plane and ECR/IAM checks (CIS 2.1.1, 5.3.1, 5.4.x, 5.5.1, ECR items, plus AWS-specific controls), and figuring out how to divide the rest.

A second sub-agent should handle node-level checks and worker-node CIS controls — launch templates, SSM, and kubelet configz via kubectl proxy — while a third focuses on the in-cluster Kubernetes API checks for CIS sections 4 and 5.x. I also want to preload only the relevant skills rather than everything, keeping in mind that some CloudTrail lookups via use_aws might be blocked.

Given the breadth of the request — a thorough, comprehensive security review across IAM, nodes, and cluster controls — this calls for full deep research mode rather than a narrow troubleshooting hunt.

{"id": "94b987d9-4066-4c77-bbff-b99ecc5d7771", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_liMWXxPhuOFcgG9fv8U0Am", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Analyze vulnerabilities in Amazon EKS\",\"context\":\"## The Center for Internet Security (CIS) benchmark for Amazon EKS\\n\\nThe Center for Internet Security (CIS) Kubernetes Benchmark provides guidance for Amazon EKS security configurations. The benchmark:\\n\\n* Is applicable to Amazon EC2 nodes (both managed and self-managed) where you are responsible for security configurations of Kubernetes components.\\n* Provides a standard, community-approved way to ensure that you have configured your Kubernetes cluster and nodes securely when using Amazon EKS.\\n* Consists of four sections; control plane logging configuration, node security configurations, policies, and managed services.\\n* Supports all of the Kubernetes versions currently available in Amazon EKS and can be run using kube-bench, a standard open source tool for checking configuration using the CIS benchmark on Kubernetes clusters.\\n\\nTo learn more, see Introducing The CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark.\\n\\nFor an automated `aws-sample` pipeline to update your node group with a CIS benchmarked AMI, see EKS-Optimized AMI Hardening Pipeline\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/configuration-vulnerability-analysis.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Protecting the infrastructure (hosts)\",\"context\":\"### Periodically run kube-bench to verify compliance with CIS benchmarks for Kubernetes\\n\\nkube-bench is an open source project from Aqua that evaluates your\\ncluster against the CIS benchmarks for Kubernetes. The benchmark\\ndescribes the best practices for securing unmanaged Kubernetes clusters.\\nThe CIS Kubernetes Benchmark encompasses the control plane and the data\\nplane. Since Amazon EKS provides a fully managed control plane, not all\\nof the recommendations from the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark are applicable.\\nTo ensure this scope reflects how Amazon EKS is implemented, AWS created\\nthe *CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark*. The EKS benchmark inherits from CIS\\nKubernetes Benchmark with additional inputs from the community with\\nspecific configuration considerations for EKS clusters.\\n\\nWhen running kube-bench\\nagainst an EKS cluster, follow\\nthese\\ninstructions from Aqua Security. For further information see\\nIntroducing\\nThe CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/protecting-the-infrastructure.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Image security\",\"context\":\"### Scan images for vulnerabilities regularly\\n\\nLike their virtual machine counterparts, container images can contain\\nbinaries and application libraries with vulnerabilities or develop\\nvulnerabilities over time. The best way to safeguard against exploits is\\nby regularly scanning your images with an image scanner. Images that are\\nstored in Amazon ECR can be scanned on push or on-demand (once during a\\n24 hour period). ECR currently supports\\ntwo\\ntypes of scanning - Basic and Enhanced. Basic scanning leverages\\nClair an open source image scanning\\nsolution for no cost.\\nEnhanced\\nscanning uses Amazon Inspector to provide automatic continuous scans\\nfor additional cost. After an\\nimage is scanned, the results are logged to the event stream for ECR in\\nEventBridge. You can also see the results of a scan from within the ECR\\nconsole. Images with a HIGH or CRITICAL vulnerability should be deleted\\nor rebuilt. If an image that has been deployed develops a vulnerability,\\nit should be replaced as soon as possible.\\n\\nKnowing where images with vulnerabilities have been deployed is\\nessential to keeping your environment secure. While you could\\nconceivably build an image tracking solution yourself, there are already\\nseveral commercial offerings that provide this and other advanced\\ncapabilities out of the box, including:\\n\\n* Grype\\n* Palo\\n Alto - Prisma Cloud (twistcli)\\n* Aqua\\n* Kubei\\n* Trivy\\n* Snyk\\n\\nA Kubernetes validation webhook could also be used to validate that\\nimages are free of critical vulnerabilities. Validation webhooks are\\ninvoked prior to the Kubernetes API. They are typically used to reject\\nrequests that don\u2019t comply with the validation criteria defined in the\\nwebhook.\\nThis\\nis an example of a serverless webhook that calls the ECR\\ndescribeImageScanFindings API to determine whether a pod is pulling an\\nimage with critical vulnerabilities. If vulnerabilities are found, the\\npod is rejected and a message with list of CVEs is returned as an Event\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/image-security.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Check CIS EKS Benchmark v1.8.0 control numbering", "parent_id": "03790c82-861e-4cec-a832-d2fdc0a3e171"}

| ID | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| AWS-1 audit logging | **FAIL** | Log group `/aws/eks/cis-skill-test/cluster` exists and `api` logs are flowing, but only 1 of 5 log types is on. Retention is never-expire. |
| AWS-2 cluster version support | **PASS** | 1.37 is in standard support until 2027-12-01 and extended support until 2028-12-01. |
| AWS-3 node group version | **PASS** | The node group runs 1.37 like the control plane, on release `1.37.1-20261112` (newest 1.37 AL2023 AMI I found). Status is ACTIVE with no health issues. |
| AWS-4 GuardDuty EKS protection | **PASS** | The detector is enabled with `EKS_AUDIT_LOGS` and `RUNTIME_MONITORING` on. The `aws-guardduty-agent` add-on v1.17.4 is ACTIVE with 2 agent pods running. |

None are in this account's ECR, so no scanner covers them. Inspector covers the nodes: 33 active findings (4 high, 27 medium, 2 low), all on the node OS and packages, not container images. |

## Biggest fixes
1. Remove or tighten the `wildcard-operator` binding for `contractors`, `ops-admin`, and the `legacy-admin` mapping to `system:masters`. That clears most of the 4.1.x failures.
2. Enable all 5 control plane log types and add KMS encryption for Secrets.
3. Restrict or disable the public endpoint, and move nodes to private subnets.
4. Turn on network policy enforcement in the VPC CNI and add policies to every namespace.
5. Remove `priv-pod` and `hostnet-pod`, and apply Pod Security Admission to `team-a` and `default`.
6. Encrypt node volumes through the launch template, and set up AWS Backup.
